tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot, spicy, and fragrant.
She likes hiking mountain trails and to swim in cold lakes.
Volunteers must arrive early, sign the register, and wearing a badge.
The guide was both patient and she explained every landmark.
He enjoys reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking bread.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three adjectives share the same form after "was," so the list is parallel.

Tip: When listing qualities, keep each item the same part of speech.

FALSE — A gerund ("hiking") is paired with an infinitive ("to swim").

Tip: After likes, stay with -ing throughout: hiking… and swimming…

FALSE — Two bare infinitives after "must" are followed by a participle ("wearing").

Tip: Shared modals need the same bare form: wear, not wearing.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an adjective to a full clause.

Tip: Match structures after both…and: both patient and clear.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "enjoys" stay in matching -ing form.

Tip: Prefer reading…, sketching…, and baking… rather than mixing with to-infinitives.
highlights: reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking
tasks.solution_overview: Read each sentence as a list or a paired construction. Ask whether every item shares the same grammatical shape. Correlatives such as both…and are correct only when the two sides match.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist mixed jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock.
Their weekend plan was to visit museums, trying new cafés, and walk along the river.
Maya is good at repairing bikes but weak in organising toolkits.
The course aims to build stamina, improve balance, and boosting confidence.
Tom likes watering the garden and pruning the hedges.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three noun phrases sit in the same pattern after "mixed."

Tip: Noun lists are parallel when each item is the same kind of noun phrase.

FALSE — An infinitive series is broken by the gerund "trying."

Tip: After "to," keep bare infinitives: visit, try, and walk.

TRUE — Adjective + preposition + gerund appears on both sides.

Tip: Parallel comparisons often reuse the same preposition pattern (at… / in…).

FALSE — The final item shifts from infinitives to a gerund ("boosting").

Tip: Finish the series with boost, not boosting.

TRUE — Two gerund phrases after "likes" match cleanly.

Tip: Prefer watering… and pruning… rather than mixing -ing with to-infinitives.
highlights: jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock
tasks.solution_overview: Check lists of nouns, infinitives, and gerunds one item at a time. A single mismatched form is enough to mark the sentence false, even if the meaning is clear.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The leaflet explains how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find the platform.
Ideal flatmates should be tidy, considerate, and pay rent on time.
The club both renovated the court and installed new lights.
Our goals are finishing homework early, sleeping enough, and to exercise daily.
The judge asked whether the answers were complete, accurate, and fair.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three matching "how to" phrases keep the instructions parallel.

Tip: Repeat how to before each step when the shared frame is "explains how to."

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a verb phrase ("pay rent").

Tip: Use three adjectives, or rewrite the third as punctual with rent.

TRUE — "Both…and" links two matching past-tense verb phrases.

Tip: Place the same kind of phrase after each half of the correlative.

FALSE — Two gerunds are paired with an infinitive ("to exercise").

Tip: Keep the -ing series: finishing, sleeping, and exercising.

TRUE — Three adjectives after "were" form a clean parallel list.

Tip: After a linking verb, adjective chains should stay adjectives throughout.
highlights: how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find
both renovated the court and installed
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for adjective lists that suddenly become verbs, and for goals written as mixed gerunds and infinitives. Keep the opening pattern through the last item.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The film was long, confusing, and it bored the audience.
She not only packed the tent but also checked the weather forecast.
Passengers must queue calmly, show their tickets, and to board in groups.
Cooking requires patience, practice, and a sharp knife.
He spends weekends repairing bikes, coaching juniors, and to race himself.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a full clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: long, confusing, and dull.

TRUE — "Not only…but also" joins two matching past-tense verb phrases.

Tip: Keep the same verb shape after each half of the correlative.

FALSE — Two bare infinitives after "must" are followed by a to-infinitive.

Tip: After must, stay bare: board, not to board.

TRUE — Three noun phrases after "requires" sit in parallel.

Tip: Noun lists after requires/needs are usually the safest parallel choice.

FALSE — Two gerunds are paired with an infinitive ("to race").

Tip: Use racing himself to keep the -ing pattern.
highlights: not only packed the tent but also checked
patience, practice, and a sharp knife
tasks.solution_overview: Warm-up items mix adjective lists, correlatives, and shared modals. Name the first item's form, then reject any ending that cannot wear the same grammatical clothes.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hike was rewarding because of the views, because of the fresh air, and the group was cheerful.
Either leave your bags in the locker or carry them with you at all times.
The recipe calls for chopping the onions, frying the spices, and to simmer the sauce.
Spectators clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved homemade banners.
She wants a laptop that is light, that is quiet, and affordable.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use because of the cheerful group so every reason stays a noun phrase.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives with the same subject.

Tip: Keep leave… or carry… — same subject, same verb form.

FALSE — Two gerunds after "calls for" are followed by an infinitive.

Tip: Finish with simmering the sauce to keep the gerund list.

TRUE — Three past-tense verb phrases describe the crowd in parallel.

Tip: Shared tense and subject make verb lists easy to keep balanced.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is affordable, or drop that is before all three.
highlights: clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved
tasks.solution_overview: Repeated subordinators and correlatives fail when the last branch changes shape. Check that because of, either…or, and that is appear consistently—or rewrite the whole list.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting between sets, he avoided injury.
The museum tour was informative, interactive, and we learned about local pottery.
Parents asked the coach to explain the drills, to demonstrate each move, and feedback after practice.
Neither the rain nor the wind stopped the outdoor market.
Her weekend routine involves cycling to the bakery, collecting the newspaper, and she waters the plants.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: informative, interactive, and memorable.

FALSE — Two infinitives after "asked…to" are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add to give feedback after practice to keep the infinitive series.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching noun phrases as a compound subject.

Tip: Keep both sides the same category: noun + noun, not noun + clause.

FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use watering the plants so every item stays a gerund.
highlights: By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting
Neither the rain nor the wind
tasks.solution_overview: Means lists with by + gerund and correlatives like neither…nor are clean when the pattern repeats. Trailing clauses after adjective or gerund pairs are the usual false marks here.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The role of team captain involves motivating players, planning practices, and attendance at matches.
We are looking for someone who can think clearly, act calmly, and speak kindly.
The prize will be used both to buy new books and decorating the reading corner.
His strengths are curiosity, humour, and solving puzzles quickly.
The committee voted to approve the mural, to hire a local artist, and to schedule the unveiling.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by a noun phrase ("attendance").

Tip: Use attending matches to keep the gerund pattern.

TRUE — Three bare infinitives after "can" form a matching series.

Tip: Shared modals (can/must/should) demand the same bare verb form each time.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an infinitive to a gerund.

Tip: Both to buy… and to decorate…, or both buying… and decorating…

FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a gerund phrase.

Tip: Use quick puzzle-solving so all three items are nouns.

TRUE — Three infinitives after "voted to" stay in parallel.

Tip: Repeating "to" before each verb is optional but often clearer.
highlights: think clearly, act calmly, and speak
both to buy new books and decorating
to approve the mural, to hire
tasks.solution_overview: Duty lists and "both…and" often hide mixed nouns, gerunds, and infinitives. Convert every item into the same type before you judge the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The campaign was effective in raising awareness, in recruiting helpers, and donations increased.
Applicants must either enclose a sketchbook or they submit a link to an online gallery.
The chef is known for bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions.
We aim not only to finish the trail but also the photos for the blog.
The workshop taught participants to define goals, to map their route, and to pack a first-aid kit.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "in + gerund" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Keep the preposition pattern: in raising…, in recruiting…, and in increasing donations.

FALSE — "Either…or" joins a bare infinitive to a full clause with a new subject.

Tip: Either enclose a sketchbook or submit a link — same subject, same verb form.

TRUE — Three noun phrases follow "known for" in parallel.

Tip: After "for," noun lists are usually the safest parallel choice.

FALSE — "Not only…but also" joins an infinitive to a bare noun.

Tip: Not only to finish the trail but also to edit the photos — match both halves.

TRUE — Three infinitives after "taught…to" match cleanly.

Tip: Repeat "to" when it keeps each learning outcome equally weighted.
highlights: bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions
to define goals, to map their route, and to pack
tasks.solution_overview: Correlatives fail when one side is a phrase and the other is a clause, or when one side has "to" and the other does not. Balance the two halves before you look at meaning.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The contest requires entrants to submit a photo, to write a short caption, and a signed consent form.
Whether by bus, by bike, or on foot, students must reach the hall by nine.
The renovation plan is ambitious, controversial, and it may stall.
She speaks fluently in Spanish, in Italian, and Portuguese.
The app can track sleep, count steps, and remind users to drink water.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives are followed by a noun phrase without "to provide/submit."

Tip: Add to include a signed consent form, or turn all three into nouns after "submit."

TRUE — Three prepositional routes stay parallel after "whether."

Tip: Keep the same preposition pattern (by… / by… / on…) when listing channels.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: ambitious, controversial, and risky.

FALSE — "In" appears before the first two languages but not the third.

Tip: Repeat in before Portuguese, or drop in before all three.

TRUE — Three bare infinitives after "can" form a matching list.

Tip: Shared auxiliaries make parallel verb lists especially clear.
highlights: by bus, by bike, or on foot
track sleep, count steps, and remind
tasks.solution_overview: Missing repeated prepositions and trailing clauses after adjective pairs are subtler errors. Read the list aloud; an abrupt change of rhythm usually signals a break in form.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach argued that fitness was improving, that teamwork was stronger, and morale was high.
She prefers walking in the park to cycle along the busy ring road.
The festival offered live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials.
Not only did they repair the roof, but they also painted the shutters.
His advice was to arrive early, sitting near the aisle, and leave during the interval.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before morale was high.

FALSE — "Prefer A to B" needs matching forms; walking is paired with cycle.

Tip: Prefer walking… to cycling… (two gerunds).

TRUE — Three noun phrases after "offered" stay parallel.

Tip: Event programmes often list noun objects cleanly when nothing switches to a clause.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — An infinitive series is broken by a gerund ("sitting").

Tip: Use to sit near the aisle to keep the infinitive pattern.
highlights: live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials
tasks.solution_overview: Repeated that-clauses and prefer…to constructions need matching markers on every branch. Prefer A to B fails when one side is -ing and the other is a bare infinitive.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notice forbids smoking indoors, bringing pets, and to leave bicycles in the hallway.
As much as she loves painting landscapes, she loves photographing them too.
The librarian asked whether the books were returned, whether fines were paid, and cards renewed.
He is neither interested in chess nor in collecting stamps.
To cook well, to plate neatly, and cleaning the kitchen quickly are all part of the shift.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two gerunds after "forbids" are followed by an infinitive.

Tip: Use leaving bicycles… so every banned action is a gerund.

TRUE — "As much as…" balances two matching "loves + gerund" clauses.

Tip: Correlative as much as often needs mirrored verb + complement patterns.

FALSE — Two "whether" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "whether."

Tip: Repeat whether before cards were renewed.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching "in + gerund/noun" phrases after "interested."

Tip: Keep the same preposition after neither and nor.

FALSE — Two infinitive subjects are followed by a gerund subject.

Tip: Use to clean the kitchen quickly so all three subjects are infinitives.
highlights: As much as she loves painting
neither interested in chess nor in collecting
tasks.solution_overview: Verb bans, whether-chains, and infinitive subjects look fine until the last item switches form. Treat the first branch as a template and force every later branch to copy it.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The brochure promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that tickets will be refundable.
Whether to reschedule the match, whether to move indoors, or cancelling altogether was debated for hours.
She left early because of a headache, because of the noise, and because her phone battery had died.
The trainer emphasised warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking enough water.
His reply was polite, brief, and unexpectedly helpful.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use refundable tickets as a third noun phrase.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to cancel altogether keeps the pattern.

FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by a because-clause.

Tip: Use because of a dead phone battery so every reason stays a noun phrase—or rewrite all three as clauses.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "emphasised" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — Three adjectives after "was" form a clean parallel list.

Tip: Adverbs like unexpectedly can modify an adjective without breaking the list.
highlights: and that tickets will be refundable
warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking
tasks.solution_overview: Mid-band items mix brochure-style noun lists with whether-to chains and mixed reason frames. Pick one frame—nouns, whether to, or because of—and hold it through every item.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success on the course depended not so much on raw talent as practising every evening.
The neighbours debated whether to plant hedges, whether to build a fence, or installing a gate.
House rules forbid leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using the roof terrace after midnight.
Her weekend is as much about cooking for friends as it is about catching up on sleep.
The motion was neither seconded promptly nor was it discussed on the merits.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Not so much…as" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Not so much on raw talent as on practising every evening — repeat on.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to install a gate keeps the pattern.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "forbid" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — "As much…as" balances two "about + gerund" ideas with matching "it is."

Tip: Correlative as much…as often needs mirrored about-phrases.

FALSE — "Neither…nor" joins a past participle phrase to an inverted clause.

Tip: Neither seconded promptly nor discussed on the merits — two past participles.
highlights: leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using
as much about cooking for friends as it is about
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced correlatives (not so much…as, as much…as, whether to…) fail when the second half drops a preposition or switches to a different verb form. Match the scaffolding, not just the topic.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The flyer promises visitors free entry, guided tours, and that parking will be available nearby.
By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding folders, and by clearing the desk nightly, she found her keys faster.
The candidate was praised for how she handled questions, how she framed answers, and her closing thank-you.
We will either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone the sewing circle until Friday.
The rule requires that guests sign in, that they leave keys at reception, and bikes be locked outside.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use nearby parking as a third noun phrase.

TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two "how" clauses are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add how she delivered her closing thank-you to keep the how-pattern.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives after "will."

Tip: Shared will + either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides.

FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before bikes be locked outside.
highlights: and that parking will be available
By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding
either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone
tasks.solution_overview: Flyer language and house rules often stack that-clauses. If that appears twice, the third clause almost always needs it too—or all three should be rewritten as nouns.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The strategy rests less on expensive kit than practising basic drills.
Not only did attendance rise in spring, but energy levels also improved.
Readers asked for a guide that is clear, that is illustrated, and useful without jargon.
The club prefers meeting outdoors on Saturdays and to convene indoors on rainy Sundays.
A solid packing list must specify what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Less…than" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Less on expensive kit than on practising basic drills.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is useful without jargon.

FALSE — A gerund ("meeting") is paired with an infinitive ("to convene").

Tip: Prefer meeting… and convening…, or to meet… and to convene…

TRUE — Three matching wh-infinitive phrases specify wear, carry, and leave.

Tip: Parallel wh-phrases are ideal for lists that must answer what and when.
highlights: what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave
tasks.solution_overview: Comparative frames (less…than) and relative-clause chains demand the same marker on every branch. When in doubt, rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The flatshare rules cover quiet hours, shared cleaning, and guests must leave by eleven.
She trains both in the gym and when the weather allows outdoor runs.
The quiz tracked page views, session duration, and how long users stayed on each question.
To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect their time are shared priorities.
The teacher advised against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing the last set.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun objects are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use an eleven o'clock guest curfew so every item stays a noun phrase.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins a prepositional phrase to a when-clause.

Tip: Both in the gym and in the park — two prepositional phrases.

FALSE — Two noun objects are followed by a how-clause.

Tip: Use question dwell time so all three metrics are noun phrases.

TRUE — Three infinitive phrases function as a parallel compound subject.

Tip: Infinitive subjects can be parallel when every infinitive carries the same role.

TRUE — Three matching "against + gerund" phrases follow "advised."

Tip: Repeating against before each gerund locks the parallel pattern.
highlights: and guests must leave by eleven
both in the gym and when
To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect
against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing
tasks.solution_overview: House rules and tracking language mix nouns, infinitives, and clauses freely in drafts. Your job is to refuse that mixing: pick one frame and hold it through every item.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The recovery hinged not so much on longer rests as rebuilding confidence through light sessions.
Organisers debated whether to delay the start, whether to shorten the route, or cancelling the race.
Hostel rules forbid accepting strangers' parcels, soliciting room swaps, and using the roof terrace after midnight.
Her weekend is as much about rebuilding trust with neighbours as it is about catching up on sleep.
The complaint was neither acknowledged promptly nor was it investigated in full.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Not so much…as" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Not so much on longer rests as on rebuilding confidence — repeat on.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to cancel the race keeps the pattern.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "forbid" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — "As much…as" balances two "about + gerund/noun" ideas with matching "it is."

Tip: Correlative as much…as often needs mirrored about-phrases.

FALSE — "Neither…nor" joins a past participle phrase to an inverted clause.

Tip: Neither acknowledged promptly nor investigated in full — two past participles.
highlights: accepting strangers' parcels, soliciting room swaps, and using
as much about rebuilding trust with neighbours as it is about
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced correlatives (not so much…as, as much…as, whether to…) fail when the second half drops a preposition or switches verb form. Match the scaffolding, not just the topic.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival flyer promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that shuttle buses will run until midnight.
By training marshals early, by publishing diversion signs, and by checking radios hourly, the walk reduced delays.
The speaker was praised for how she handled hecklers, how she timed jokes, and her encore story.
We will either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone the project until spring.
The campsite asks that visitors log arrivals, that they sort recycling carefully, and fires be extinguished by ten.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use midnight shuttle buses as a third noun phrase.

TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two "how" clauses are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add how she delivered her encore story to keep the how-pattern.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives after "will."

Tip: Shared will + either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides.

FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before fires be extinguished by ten.
highlights: and that shuttle buses will run
By training marshals early, by publishing
either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone
tasks.solution_overview: Festival flyers and campsite rules often stack that-clauses. If that appears twice, the third clause almost always needs it too—or all three should be rewritten as nouns.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Good bread rests less on exotic flour than kneading the dough with patience.
Not only did attendance rise after Easter, but energy levels also improved.
Campers asked for a trail note that is realistic, that is waterproof, and useful without jargon.
The choir prefers rehearsing in person on Mondays and to rehearse online on Thursdays.
A solid itinerary must specify who books the tickets, what bags are allowed, and when the group will meet.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Less…than" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Less on exotic flour than on kneading the dough with patience.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is useful without jargon.

FALSE — A gerund ("rehearsing") is paired with an infinitive ("to rehearse").

Tip: Prefer rehearsing… and rehearsing online…, or to rehearse… and to rehearse…

TRUE — Three matching wh-clauses specify who, what, and when.

Tip: Parallel wh-clauses are ideal for plans that must answer ownership, contents, and timing.
highlights: who books the tickets, what bags
tasks.solution_overview: Comparative frames (less…than) and relative-clause chains demand the same marker on every branch. When in doubt, rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The landlord authorised tenants to repaint the hallway, to replace the hallway bulbs, and filing a repair request if leaks returned.
Just as the café invests in better beans, so too does it invest in staff training.
Progress will be judged on whether chores are finished, whether keys are returned, and communal lights are off.
The brief is neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss every suggestion wholesale.
She moved out because of limited daylight, because of noisy neighbours, and her commute had become unmanageable.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives after "authorised…to" are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Use to file a repair request to keep the infinitive series.

TRUE — "Just as…so too" balances two matching invest + in + noun patterns with inversion on the second clause.

Tip: Correlative just as…so too needs mirrored clause structure.

FALSE — Two "whether" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "whether."

Tip: Repeat whether before communal lights are off.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching infinitives after "is."

Tip: Keep to + bare verb on both sides of neither…nor.

FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use because of an unmanageable commute so every reason stays a noun phrase.
highlights: neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss
tasks.solution_overview: Final-band items combine correlatives, repeated subordinators, and long infinitive chains. Name the opening structure of each sentence, then reject any ending that cannot wear the same grammatical clothes.
